claim: Sepsis is associated with high morbidity and mortality.
source: Sepsis is associated with high morbidity and mortality (Singer et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Singer et al., 2016

claim: Adequate antibiotic therapy in time could decrease mortality and reduce the length of stay in ICU for patients with sepsis or septic shock.
source: Adequate antibiotic therapy in time could decrease mortality and reduce the length of stay in ICU for patients with sepsis or septic shock (Ferrer et al., 2018; Kumar et al., 2006; Pulia and Redwood, 2020; Seymour et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published studies

claim: The mortality rate of patients increased approximately 7.6% for every hour delayed in antibiotic therapy.
source: As reported in the previous study, the mortality rate of patients increased approximately 7.6% for every hour delayed (Kumar et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kumar et al., 2006

claim: Conventional culture test (CCT) is the most commonly used and golden standard identification method of pathogenic microorganisms in most countries.
source: Conventional culture test (CCT) is the most commonly used and golden standard identification method of pathogenic microorganisms in most countries.
evidence: Based on established clinical practice knowledge

claim: CCT has long time-consuming (2–5 days) and low sensitivity (30–50%) limitations.
source: However, it showed two critical limitations: long time-consuming (2–5 days) and low sensitivity (30–50%), which limited the application of this method in the ICU (Abd El-Aziz et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Abd El-Aziz et al., 2021 and Zhou et al., 2014

claim: NGS technology needs at least 2 days for the full diagnostic report with high cost.
source: However, the whole process still needs at least 2 days for the full diagnostic report with high cost (Chen et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2020 and Wang et al., 2020

claim: NGS provides too much information about microorganisms but only semi-quantification of pathogens.
source: On the other hand, NGS provided too much information about microorganisms but only semi-quantification of pathogens, which was hard for most clinical doctors to extract the most important information to determine antibiotic usage.
evidence: Based on inference about NGS limitations in clinical practice

claim: Detection techniques designed by BioFire and Curetis are superior in detection time but have potential false-positive results due to their principle based on nucleotide diversity of conserved genes.
source: Other new emerging detection techniques designed by BioFire and Curetis are much superior in detection time than these above. However, its original principle was based on nucleotide diversity of conserved genes among species, which could not satisfy the application in the ICU due to potential false-positive results (Edin et al., 2020; Jamal et al., 2014; Trotter et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Edin et al., 2020; Jamal et al., 2014; Trotter et al., 2019

claim: A total of 1791 high-quality genomes of 232 microorganism species from public databases were included in the screening process.
source: A total of 1791 high-quality genomes of 232 microorganism species from the public databases were included in the screening process.
evidence: Direct statement about the data used in the study

claim: The developed linear comparison algorithm could save more than 90% of calculation time cost.
source: To accelerate the screening process, we developed a linear comparison algorithm instead of comparing every two genomes, which could save more than 90% of calculation time cost (Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: Supported by data and reference to Appendix 1—figure 1

claim: 10 species of bacteria covered 76% sepsis pathogenic bacteria according to epidemiological data.
source: According to the epidemiological data by previous retrospective study (Zhou et al., 2014) and 2017 data in ICU of Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital (Appendix 1—figure 2), 10 species of bacteria covered 76% sepsis pathogenic bacteria and therefore were selected as targets for subsequent detecting process
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2014 and reference to Appendix 1—figure 2

claim: The 10 selected bacteria species include Acinetobacter baumannii, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus epidermidis, Staphylococcus capitis, Enterococcus faecalis and Enterococcus faecium.
source: including Acinetobacter baumannii (A. baumannii), Escherichia coli (E. coli), Klebsiella pneumoniae (K. pneumoniae), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (P. aeruginosa), Stenotrophomonas maltophilia (S. maltophilia), Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus), Staphylococcus epidermidis (S. epidermidis), Staphylococcus capitis (S. capitis), Enterococcus faecalis (E. faecalis) and Enterococcus faecium (E. faecium).
evidence: Direct statement of the selected bacteria panel

claim: Bacteria-specific DNA sequences showed a random distribution and turned out to be only 0.3–4.1% in the whole genomes of 10 bacteria.
source: To our surprise, bacteria-specific DNA sequences showed a random distribution and turned out to be only 0.3–4.1% in the whole genomes of 10 bacteria (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2B and C

claim: The lowest detection limit of SSBD was 10–15 M with PCR amplification and 10–8M without amplification step.
source: With the gradient concentration of DNA templates, we confirmed that the lowest detection limit was 10–15 M with PCR amplification and 10–8M without amplification step (Figure 3B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: 30 min incubation of CRISPR/Cas12a with PCR products was enough to demonstrate signals.
source: In addition, 30 min' incubation of CRISPR/Cas12a with PCR products was enough to demonstrate signals (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: An additional purification step right after PCR amplification appeared unnecessary to acquire the positive result but helpful for weaker signal.
source: An additional purification step right after PCR amplification appeared unnecessary to acquire the positive result but helpful for weaker signal (Appendix 1—figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Appendix 1—figure 3A

claim: Fluorescence value showed a significant difference from 5 min and reached its maximum after 30 min compared to the negative control.
source: In addition, the comparison of CRISPR/Cas incubation duration confirmed that fluorescence value showed a significant difference from 5 min and reached its maximum after 30 min compared to the negative control (Appendix 1—figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Appendix 1—figure 3B

claim: Each bacteria strain tested by 10 SSBD test panels showed positive results only for the SSBD targeting the tested bacteria, confirming high specificity.
source: To further confirm the specificity of SSBD, each bacteria strain was tested by 10 SSBD test panels targeting different bacteria. Compared to negative control, only SSBD targeting the tested bacteria showed a positive result, which confirmed its high specificity (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: In validation stage I, 77 samples of BALF were tested by both SSBD and CCT.
source: We started our study with validation stage I, which was a non-intervention study with 77 samples of BALF extracted from patients. Samples were detected both by SSBD and CCT, and the results were compared (raw detection results were shown in Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: Direct statement about the study design and sample size

claim: SSBD could detect five bacteria (A. baumannii, K. pneumoniae, P. aeruginosa, S. aureus, and S. maltophilia) separately with 100% sensitivity and over 87% specificity.
source: Generally, 5 of 10 selected bacteria were detected by both tests, including A. baumannii, K. pneumoniae, P. aeruginosa, S. aureus, and S. maltophilia. SSBD could detect those five bacteria separately with 100% sensitivity and over 87% specificity, which were calculated by the results of CCT as golden standard (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4A comparing SSBD to CCT as gold standard

claim: SSBD was highly consistent with NGS results.
source: Among all samples, 11 of them were determined by patients to acquire results with NGS, which provided extra information to evaluate the results (Appendix 1—table 4). Based on the results, SSBD was highly consistent with NGS, which implied that SSBD might provide more accurate and complete pathogenic information than CCT in the selected panel.
evidence: Based on comparison of SSBD and NGS results for 11 samples

claim: 22 patients were recruited into the experiment group and 24 patients into the control group in validation stage II.
source: Although the study was paused due to the outbreak of SARS-CoV2, 22 patients were recruited into the experiment group and 24 patients into the control group.
evidence: Direct statement about patient recruitment numbers

claim: The baseline characteristics had no significant difference except ages between the two groups.
source: The baseline characteristics had no significant difference except ages (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Table 1

claim: In the experiment group, 47 samples were positive among 57 samples tested by SSBD, while 28 samples were positive among 43 samples tested by CCT.
source: In the experiment group, 47 samples were positive among 57 samples tested by SSBD, while 28 samples were positive among 43 samples tested by CCT (raw detection results were shown in Appendix 1—table 5).
evidence: Direct statement of detection results with reference to raw data

claim: In the control group, 41 samples showed positive among 63 samples.
source: In the control group, 41 samples showed positive among 63 samples.
evidence: Direct statement of detection results

claim: SSBD could detect each bacterium with similar high sensitivity and specificity in validation stage II.
source: It was shown that SSBD could detect each bacterium with similar high sensitivity and specificity in validation stage II (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4B

claim: A. baumannii was the most frequent occurrence according to local epidemic data.
source: Consistent with the local epidemic data, the most frequent occurrence was A. baumannii (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4B and consistency with local epidemic data

claim: Effective antibiotic coverage rates for each test were significantly higher in the experimental group than those in the control group in three tests.
source: Effective antibiotic coverage rates for each test were significantly higher in the experimental group than those in the control group in three tests (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4C

claim: APACHE II scores were significantly lower in the experimental group than those in the control group after day 1 (p=0.0035, two-way ANOVA).
source: APACHE II scores were significantly lower in the experimental group than those in the control group after day 1 (p=0.0035, two-way ANOVA); the separation between two groups of patients increased progressively until day 14 (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA) of data shown in Figure 4D

claim: SOFA scores showed no difference between the groups (p=0.8918, two-way ANOVA).
source: SOFA scores showed no difference between the groups (p=0.8918, two-way ANOVA) (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA) of data shown in Figure 4E

claim: The detection rate of polymicrobial infection events by SSBD was 41.8% (55/134) in two validation stages.
source: From the results, the detection rate of polymicrobial infection events by SSBD was 41.8% (55/134) in two validation stages, which was significantly higher than 11.7% (14/120) of CCT (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5A

claim: The detection rate of polymicrobial infection events by CCT was 11.7% (14/120).
source: From the results, the detection rate of polymicrobial infection events by SSBD was 41.8% (55/134) in two validation stages, which was significantly higher than 11.7% (14/120) of CCT (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Polymicrobial infection events demonstrated high consistency between SSBD and NGS.
source: Polymicrobial infection events were compared among SSBD, CCT and NGS, which demonstrated high consistency of SSBD and NGS (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by comparison data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Both SSBD and CCT demonstrated similar results with A. baumannii, S. maltophilia, P. aeruginosa, K. pneumoniae and S. aureus in top 5 pathogens participating in polymicrobial infection events.
source: From the aspect of pathogen species participated in polymicrobial infection events, both methods demonstrated similar results with A. baumannii, S. maltophilia, P. aeruginosa, K. pneumoniae and S. aureus in top 5 (Figure 5D), which were consistent with the frequency of pathogens in ICU (De Pascale et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5D and citation to De Pascale et al., 2012

claim: 47.6% (10/21) of patients had nosocomial infections at test 2 according to SSBD results.
source: Based on the results of SSBD, 47.6% (10/21) of patients had nosocomial infections at the test 2, and 28.6% (4/14) of patients had nosocomial infections at the test 3.
evidence: Supported by data from SSBD results

claim: 28.6% (4/14) of patients had nosocomial infections at test 3 according to SSBD results.
source: Based on the results of SSBD, 47.6% (10/21) of patients had nosocomial infections at the test 2, and 28.6% (4/14) of patients had nosocomial infections at the test 3.
evidence: Supported by data from SSBD results

claim: 40% (4/10) of patients were identified as nosocomial infections by CCT at test 2.
source: Similarly, 40% (4/10) of patients were identified as nosocomial infections by CCT at test 2, and 27.3% (3/11) of patients were identified as nosocomial infections at test 3 (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5G

claim: 27.3% (3/11) of patients were identified as nosocomial infections by CCT at test 3.
source: Similarly, 40% (4/10) of patients were identified as nosocomial infections by CCT at test 2, and 27.3% (3/11) of patients were identified as nosocomial infections at test 3 (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5G

claim: Two typical strains PAO1 and PAO7 of P. aeruginosa demonstrate less than 94% nucleotide identity.
source: For example, two typical strains PAO1 and PAO7 of P. aeruginosa (NCBI representative genome database) demonstrate less than 94% nucleotide identity
evidence: Based on data from NCBI representative genome database

claim: E. coli and Shigella sonnei representative genomes share more than 98% nucleotide identity.
source: while E. coli and Shigella sonnei both belong to Enterobateriaceae and their representative genomes share more than 98% nucleotide identity.
evidence: Based on genome comparison data

claim: Patients in the experiment group had quicker directed therapy adjustment (10.2±8.8 hours) compared to control group (96.0±35.1 hr, p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney test).
source: When evaluating the clinical benefit from SSBD, the quicker directed therapy adjustment for patients in the experiment group (Exp: 10.2±8.8 hours vs. Con: 96.0±35.1 hr, p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney test)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney test) of clinical data

claim: CCT has defects in the evaluation of polymicrobial infection events due to the limitations of its technology.
source: Based on the previous studies, CCT had defects in the evaluation of polymicrobial infection events due to the limitations of its technology (Azevedo et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Azevedo et al., 2017

claim: Hospital infections are an important factor in the incidence rate and mortality of ICU patients with severe pneumonia.
source: Hospital infections, also known as nosocomial infections, are an important factor in the incidence rate and mortality of ICU patients with severe pneumonia (Zaragoza et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zaragoza et al., 2020

claim: Polymicrobial pneumonia is related to an increased risk of inappropriate antimicrobial treatment.
source: Previous studies showed that polymicrobial pneumonia is related to an increased risk of inappropriate antimicrobial treatment (Karner et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Karner et al., 2020

claim: Bacteria are quite similar between close-related species but sometimes quite different among different strains of one species due to fast evolution and horizontal gene transfer.
source: Bacteria were quite similar between close-related species but sometimes quite different among different strains of one species due to fast evolution and horizontal gene transfer (Dombrowski et al., 2020; Brito, 2021; Groussin et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to Dombrowski et al., 2020; Brito, 2021; Groussin et al., 2021

claim: The lowest detection limit of 10–15 M with PCR amplification was consistent with previous studies.
source: With the gradient concentration of DNA templates, we confirmed that the lowest detection limit was 10–15 M with PCR amplification and 10–8M without amplification step (Figure 3B), which was consistent with previous studies (Gootenberg et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Gootenberg et al., 2018

claim: SSBD can complete the detection process in 4 hours.
source: In the validation stage I, 77 BALF samples were tested, and SSBD could identify designated organisms in 4 hr with almost 100% sensitivity and over 87% specific rate.
evidence: Direct statement about detection time in validation stage I

claim: SSBD results were obtained in 4 hr in validation stage II, leading to better APACHE II scores (p=0.0035, ANOVA test).
source: In validation stage II, the SSBD results were obtained in 4 hr, leading to better APACHE II scores (p=0.0035, ANOVA test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA test) of clinical outcome data

claim: Cultivation results could deviate from the real pathogenic situation with polymicrobial infections based on SSBD results.
source: Based on the results acquired by SSBD, cultivation results could deviate from the real pathogenic situation with polymicrobial infections.
evidence: Based on inference from comparing SSBD and cultivation results

claim: Nosocomial infections were found widely in ICU.
source: In addition, nosocomial infections were found widely in ICU, which should deserve more attention.
evidence: Based on data from the study showing nosocomial infection rates

claim: SSBD was confirmed to be a powerful tool for severe pneumonia diagnosis in ICU with high accuracy.
source: SSBD was confirmed to be a powerful tool for severe pneumonia diagnosis in ICU with high accuracy.
evidence: Based on overall results from validation stages I and II

claim: The study was funded by National Natural Science Foundation of China with project number 81927808.
source: Funding:National Natural Science Foundation of China. The National Key Scientific Instrument and Equipment Development Project. Project number: 81927808.
evidence: Direct statement about funding source

claim: The study was registered at https://clinicaltrials.gov/ (NCT04178382).
source: Clinical trial number:This study was registered at https://clinicaltrials.gov/ (NCT04178382).
evidence: Direct statement about clinical trial registration

claim: Patients admitted to ICUs and diagnosed with severe pneumonia were recruited from Aug 27, 2019.
source: Patients admitted to ICUs and diagnosed with severe pneumonia were recruited from Aug 27, 2019.
evidence: Direct statement about patient recruitment start date

claim: A sample size of 73 patients in each group was needed according to sample size calculation.
source: According to previous mortality acquired from the adequate anti-infective group, the sample size calculation (two-group rate) for patients was done, and a sample size of 73 patients in each group was needed.
evidence: Based on statistical sample size calculation

claim: BALFs were obtained from all patients on day 1, day 3–5, and day 7–10 after recruitment.
source: BALFs were obtained from all the patients from 2 groups on day 1, day 3–5, and day 7–10 after recruitment and were sent directly to the hospital diagnostic microbiology laboratory for CCT and susceptibility testing.
evidence: Direct statement about sample collection schedule

claim: CCT results were obtained in strict accordance with international ERS/ESICM/ESCMID/ALAT guidelines for the management of hospital-acquired pneumonia and ventilator-associated pneumonia.
source: CCT results were obtained in strict accordance with international ERS/ESICM/ESCMID/ALAT guidelines for the management of hospital-acquired pneumonia and ventilator-associated pneumonia, which is currently the guideline for clinical gold standard.
evidence: Direct statement about adherence to clinical guidelines

claim: SSBD provided a lower threshold of detection (10–15 M) than CCT.
source: SSBD provided a lower threshold of detection (10–15 M) than CCT, which could detect pathogens that even existed in trace amounts which unable to be cultivated.
evidence: Based on comparison of detection limits between SSBD and CCT

claim: The fluorescence intensity obtained from SSBD was divided into three intervals representing different strengths of bacteria.
source: In our study, the fluorescence intensity obtained from SSBD was divided into three intervals (level I: 10–15-10–14 M, level II: 10–14 M-10–13 M, level III: over 10–13 M), representing the different strengths of bacteria (roughly equivalent to bacteria amounts according to our lowest detection thresholds, dividing details in SSBD diagnostic report of Appendix 1).
evidence: Direct statement about the classification system used in SSBD

claim: A. baumannii was found to be the most competitive bacteria in cultivation, which may be due to its fastest growth rate.
source: For example, A. baumannii was found to be the most competitive bacteria in cultivation, which may be due to its fastest growth rate.
evidence: Based on inference from cultivation results and bacterial growth characteristics

claim: P. aeruginosa seemed to be relatively the weakest one in cultivation, usually concealed with other species existing.
source: On the other hand, P. aeruginosa seemed to be relatively the weakest one among them, which was usually concealed in the cultivation with other species existing (sample A16, B19-3, B21-1, B21-2 after we excluded all samples with A. baumannii existing).
evidence: Based on inference from cultivation results of specific samples

claim: Patients in experiment groups demonstrated significant better measures of temperature improvement at day 3 and WBC improvement at day 7.
source: As showed in Appendix 1—table 8, patients in experiment groups for example demonstrated significant better measures of temperature improvement at day 3, WBC improvement at day 7.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Appendix 1—table 8

claim: At the endpoint, clinical outcomes showed no differences between the two groups, which may be due to insufficient patient numbers.
source: Nevertheless, at the endpoint, clinical outcomes showed no differences between the two groups, which may due to the insufficient patient numbers.
evidence: Based on clinical outcome data and speculation about sample size

claim: Multi-drug resistant organisms (MDROs) prevailed in ICU.
source: Multi-drug resistant organisms (MDROs) prevailed in ICU (Liu et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to Liu et al., 2020 and Yang et al., 2020

claim: SSBD provided more timely information for clinical control and response compared to CCT for nosocomial infections.
source: Although SSBD identified similar ratio of nosocomial infection events with CCT (Figure 5G), SSBD provided more timely information for clinical control and response, which might improve the clinical medication decision in ICU.
evidence: Based on inference from comparison of detection times between SSBD and CCT

claim: SSBD is associated with more rapid administration of appropriate antimicrobial therapy in the experiment cases.
source: As anticipated, SSBD performed well with high sensitivity and specificity in rapid pathogens identification, and it possessed shorter turnover time, which was associated with more rapid administration of appropriate antimicrobial therapy in the experiment cases.
evidence: Based on clinical data showing faster therapy adjustment times

claim: SSBD has enormous potential in expanding pathogens from different diseases with much more pathogen genomes included.
source: SSBD also has enormous potential in expanding pathogens from different diseases with much more pathogen genomes included.
evidence: Speculative statement about future applications

claim: The study was paused due to the outbreak of SARS-CoV2.
source: Although the study was paused due to the outbreak of SARS-CoV2, 22 patients were recruited into the experiment group and 24 patients into the control group.
evidence: Direct statement about study interruption

claim: DNA amplified sequences from S. aureus and S. epidermidis used by FilmArray Pneumonia Panel had highly similar DNA sequences in the S. epidermidis representative genome.
source: For example, sequences used by FilmArray Pneumonia Panel from two gene regions had highly similar DNA sequences in the S. epidermidis representative genome (E-value=5e-40, rpoB; E-value=8e-39, gyrB), which could interfere with pathogen identification between species from the same genus.
evidence: Based on sequence alignment data showing E-values

claim: Sequences used for S. aureus diagnosis by SSBD had no similar fragments in S. epidermidis.
source: It was shown that our sequences used for S. aureus diagnosis had no similar fragments in S. epidermidis, which avoided distinguishing different species by gene diversity.
evidence: Based on sequence alignment analysis

claim: SSBD can quantify bacterial load based on fluorescence intensity for better antibiotic therapy strategy.
source: Therefore, our SSBD method seemed more advantageous in time-consuming and information effectiveness than other mentioned methods, especially when we could quantify bacterial load based on fluorescence intensity for better antibiotic therapy strategy.
evidence: Based on the fluorescence intensity measurement capability of SSBD

claim: CRISPR/Cas12a shows robustness and lower equipment requirement compared to qPCR.
source: CRISPR/Cas12a and qPCR are both quantitative methods, but CRISPR/Cas12a shows its robustness and lower equipment requirement, which satisfied our needs for most of the ICU.
evidence: Based on comparison of technical requirements between methods

claim: S. maltophilia was detected as level II in test1 with SSBD but not CCT in patient B19.
source: Here, we showed patient B19 as an example, who received three times tests at days 1, 3, and 7 by both CCT and SSBD. Based on the results, S. maltophilia was detected as level II in test1 with SSBD but not CCT.
evidence: Based on specific patient case data

claim: S. maltophilia was detected by CCT in test2 in patient B19 after development from level II to level III based on SSBD results.
source: Later on, S. maltophilia was detected by CCT in test2 as well with few days' development from level II to level III based on result of SSBD, which means SSBD discovered the true polymicrobial infection event earlier than CCT (Figure 5C).
evidence: Based on specific patient case data shown in Figure 5C

claim: SSBD discovered the true polymicrobial infection event earlier than CCT in patient B19.
source: Later on, S. maltophilia was detected by CCT in test2 as well with few days' development from level II to level III based on result of SSBD, which means SSBD discovered the true polymicrobial infection event earlier than CCT (Figure 5C).
evidence: Based on inference from temporal comparison of detection results

claim: Appropriate antibiotic treatment guided by in-time pathogenic information would alleviate acute physiological illness.
source: It implied that appropriate antibiotic treatment guided by in-time pathogenic information would alleviate acute physiological illness.
evidence: Based on inference from clinical outcome data showing improved APACHE II scores

claim: The 10 designed pathogens were originated from sepsis, which might not completely overlap with pathogens of severe pneumonia.
source: The 10 designed pathogens were originated from sepsis, which might not completely overlap with pathogens of severe pneumonia, though pneumonia is one of the most common causes of sepsis.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential limitation of pathogen panel selection

claim: Other potential pathogenic microbes, such as viruses and fungus, might affect the clinical outcomes considering the complexity of ICU patients.
source: Other potential pathogenic microbes, such as viruses and fungus, might affect the clinical outcomes considering the complexity of ICU patients.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential confounding factors

claim: Resistance genes were not included in the study.
source: Despite the size in our intervention stage, there were still some aspects that have not been considered. (1) Resistance genes were not included in the study.

claim: The panel pathogens could be optimized flexibly for meeting diverse clinical needs in the ICU.
source: The panel pathogens could be optimized flexibly for meeting diverse clinical needs in the ICU.
